prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Memory from EARLIER parts of the document (do not extract facts from it; use it only to resolve names, aliases and who produces an item):
Context: FAA NextGen program aims to increase capacity/efficiency of the National Airspace System (NAS). En route operations are efficient in fair weather (area navigation, direct routing via air traffic automation upgrades) but suffer in adverse weather (convection/thunderstorms, winds, turbulence, snow/ice, visibility/low ceilings; ~70% of US delays; 32,000 min average NAS delay summer 2014). Actors: FAA traffic managers use severe weather avoidance plans (Playbook routes), strategic plans devised 2+ hours before departure, to divert traffic around weather-impacted regions; predictable but cause large route deviations. Gap: no automation today notifies traffic managers when weather constraints change and avoidance routes may no longer be needed, leading to longer flights, more time/fuel and higher costs for flight operators and the public. Scope: a 2015 NASA stakeholder survey (industry, flight operators, others) of air traffic management (ATM) issues found weather-related delays/interruptions the most significant and costly en route problem. Future traffic demand requires a more efficient, integrated traffic management system and controller tools. System of interest: NASA Airspace Technology Demonstrations 3 (ATD-3) project, a suite of integrated ground- and aircraft-based technologies and decision-making aids intended to continuously search for more efficient weather-avoidance routes and rapidly respond to weather changes and associated traffic management initiatives (TMIs). No modes or normative requirements stated yet.

Document units:
U0014: These route efficiency enhancements are targeted at en route airspace and will enable continued use of en route and arrival metering in the presence of weather.
U0015: NASA’s Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR) concept represents a subset of those technologies and focuses primarily on the cruise phase of flight.
U0016: It leverages existing air traffic weather, airspace, and traffic data, as well as improvements in navigation, surveillance, communication and digital network technologies, and builds upon existing ATM automation to address the shortcomings associated with strategic traffic flow management initiatives and weather forecasting uncertainties.
U0017: The potential benefits in the form of time, fuel, and cost savings are significant.
U0018: This concept of operations synopsis provides a detailed description of DWR, its potential benefits and notional implementation paths. 3 CURRENT SYSTEM - SHORTFALLS In today’s operations, Traffic Management Initiatives, or TMIs, are necessary to ensure aircraft safely avoid areas of adverse weather and to meter traffic when demand in a given area exceeds air traffic control’s capacity to safely separate aircraft.
U0019: Although necessary for safety, route diversions and metering can be overly conservative due to uncertainty in weather forecasts and air traffic control capacity limitations in sectors adjacent to the weather.
U0020: When significant convective activity is forecasted to develop in an area of the NAS, FAA traffic managers identify those areas as Flow Constrained Area (FCA), and may implement Severe Weather Avoidance Plans (SWAP), or Playbook routes, to safely divert traffic around those weather-impacted regions.
U0021: Playbook routes are identified 2 to 8 hours prior to the time the constraint is predicted to develop, to provide traffic managers and aircraft operators with ample time to prepare and assign the necessary resources where needed.
U0022: This lead time combined with uncertainties in weather forecasts often results in overly conservative deviations around actual weather.
U0023: Playbook routes tend to be very conservative both geographically and temporally to account for uncertainties in forecast accuracy.
U0024: This typically results in the selected playbook routes giving predicted weather-impacted areas a wide berth to account for those forecast uncertainties, and helps minimize subsequent changes, which can be complicated and time-consuming to implement once the SWAP routes are in play.
